processing: Though it is a large-leaf variety of the kind usually suited to black tea, it is made entirely into green tea here, fixed and shaped into flat, fairly straight leaves.
harvest_season: Spring. Plump buds are the mark of the variety, and the premium Pipa Xianming style uses one bud and one leaf.
appearance_dry: Plump buds shaped flat and fairly straight, with a glossy yellow-green colour.
appearance_wet: Even, shining yellow-green buds and leaves.
taste_profile: A rich chestnut aroma with a fresh, mellow, clean-finishing cup that takes repeat steeps well.

brewing.notes: Plump large-leaf buds can take slightly hotter water than delicate small-leaf greens, but start short and lengthen only if the cup seems thin.

vintage_note: Sold as a green tea, so the current spring's harvest is what you want, as is usual for Sichuan greens, ideally drunk within a year. It is not an ageing tea.
description:
Do not let the name mislead you: this has nothing to do with Chongqing the city. The Chongqing here is written differently in Chinese and is the old county name of what is now Chongzhou, near Chengdu. Pipa means loquat, and the tea trees take that name because their leaves resemble loquat leaves.

This is a rare local population of tea plants that grows in the Longmen range in the north-west of Chongzhou, where it is said to do best at about 1,000 metres. It is a large-leaf variety, which usually points towards black tea, yet here it is made only into green tea.

Expect plump buds, a yellow-green tone rather than a sharp emerald one, and a strong chestnut scent. The cup is fresh and clean, with enough substance to last through several steeps. Its producers claim high levels of extract and polyphenols compared with Fuding Dabai, which fits a cup with some weight.

The protected area covers five mountain townships of Chongzhou. When buying, check for Chongzhou as the origin and for the current year's harvest. A related name you may see is Pipa Xianming, a one-bud-one-leaf tea made from this variety.
history:
Chongzhou has a long tea-growing past, and a local story says this tea once went to court as a tribute called Longmen tribute tea; that remains a tradition rather than a record. Solid dates begin in the twentieth century. In 1965 the variety was named among 21 fine Chinese tea cultivars, and in 1970 it was taken to Yongchuan for breeding work, which after eight years gave the selection Chongpi 71-1.

In 1985 Sichuan's cultivar committee counted it among the province's five fine local varieties. When Chongpi 71-1 was brought back and trialled from 1993, it budded 10 to 15 days later than the parent and gave fewer steeps. Pipa Xianming, developed from the local trees, won provincial and city quality awards in 1994.

The tea was registered as a protected agricultural geographical indication on 27 May 2009, and a Chongqing Pipa tea garden is listed as a cultural relic site by the city of Chengdu.
